summary: Describes a framework for sending only the changes to an XML document, rather than a full new copy. Each change is located using an XPath selector that points at the part of the document to add, replace, or remove. It gives other protocols a common way to express partial updates to XML data.

eli5.summary: Instead of mailing a whole new book when one page changes, you send a note saying go to page 12 and swap this sentence. The reader makes the fix, and nobody resends the whole book.

questions: how to send only changes to an xml document
what is the xml patch framework
what does the sel attribute do in xml patch
subtitle: A small set of add, replace and remove operations, aimed with XPath, for sending only the changes to an XML document.

tldr.problem: Without a way to mark only the changed parts, sending an update to an XML document means sending a whole new copy.
tldr.mechanism: A diff document holds add, replace and remove elements. Each has a 'sel' attribute, a restricted XPath 1.0 selector that locates one node, and the new content sits inside the element.
tldr.outcome: It is a building block rather than a full diff format. Other specifications embed it, and it defines an error format for patches that cannot be applied.

today: RFC 5261 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of this patch framework for specifications such as RFC 5262 that build on it.

sections.title: Why Patch XML
sections.content:
XML documents are widely used to exchange and store data. To send a change, the sender normally has to send a full copy of the new version unless there is a way to indicate only the parts that changed. RFC 5261 describes such a way: an XML patch framework that uses XPath selectors to point at the part of the document to change.

It deliberately does not define a full XML diff format. It defines only the basic patch operation elements, which are meant to be embedded inside a full format that adds its own semantics. The RFC gives examples: the partial PIDF format of RFC 5262 for SIP-based presence, SIP event notification (RFC 3265), and XCAP resources (RFC 4825).

The framework can add, replace or remove elements, attributes, namespaces, comments, texts and processing instructions. It cannot patch the full XML prolog (including entities) or the document root node, and it cannot add or remove the root element. Comments and processing instructions of the root node may be patched.
sections.eli5: It is a tiny toolbox for editing a document from far away: add something, swap something, or take something out.

sections.title: Diff Documents and Selectors
sections.content:
An XML diff document contains patch operation elements, namespace declarations and the new content needed to turn a target XML document into a patched XML document. The operations are applied one after another in document order, and each result becomes the document the next patch works on.

Every operation has a sel attribute holding an XPath selector from a restricted subset of XPath 1.0. It must locate exactly one node; finding several is an error. Selectors start at the document root, so relative paths SHOULD be used. Typical selectors combine element names, attribute value predicates, text values, positional constraints such as [2], and optionally the id() function when the schema or xml:id supplies ID attributes.

Applications choose their own selector style. Positional selectors are shortest but fragile, because indexes shift after removals and insertions. Name-plus-attribute selectors are easier for tools to generate but give larger diff documents. A diff document SHOULD contain only modified nodes, and applications decide how to generate and version them.
sections.eli5: The selector is the address on the envelope. It must point to exactly one spot in the document, like "third drawer, second folder", or the patch cannot be applied.

sections.title: The Add, Replace and Remove Operations
sections.content:
add puts new content (the element's children) into the document. With no extra attributes, the children are appended as the last children of the located element. The optional pos attribute changes placement: prepend makes them the first children, before and after make them the immediately preceding or following siblings. To add an attribute or namespace declaration, type is set to @attr or namespace::pref and the content is a single text node holding the value or namespace URI.

replace has only sel. Replacing an element, comment or processing instruction needs a child of the same type. Replacing an attribute value, a namespace URI or text uses text content, and an empty replace leaves an empty attribute value, or removes a text node. Replacing an element removes all its old descendants, attributes and namespace declarations.

remove deletes the located node, and an element goes with all of its contents. The optional ws attribute (before, after or both) also removes adjacent white space text nodes, and it is an error if one is required but missing. It is not allowed for text, attribute and namespace nodes.

Because XPath forbids two adjacent text nodes, text next to an inserted or removed node is merged so that the canonical form of the result stays deterministic.
sections.eli5: There are three moves: put something in, swap something out, or throw something away. Each move says exactly which spot it is about.

sections.title: Namespace Handling
sections.content:
Prefixes are local, so the diff document and the target document may use different prefixes for the same namespace. The processor MUST resolve prefixes separately in each document and compare the resulting namespace URIs. The diff document MUST declare every namespace it uses.

This differs from plain XPath: in this framework a selector with no prefix matches only an element whose namespace (or lack of one) matches exactly. When there is a default namespace in the diff document, an unprefixed name is evaluated in it. The XPath functions namespace-uri() and local-name() are not allowed in selectors.

When new content uses a namespace, the processor MUST make sure the patched document carries it, rewriting prefixes if needed. If several prefixes in the target are bound to the same namespace, there are ordered rules: use the diff's prefix if the target has it, then the prefix of the evaluation context node, then the closest preceding prefix in an alphabetical list. The patched document MUST NOT be cleaned up to drop unused namespace declarations.
sections.eli5: Two people can call the same friend by different nicknames. The patch tool checks who the friend really is, not the nickname.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
If any patch operation cannot be fulfilled unambiguously, that is an error, and processing the remaining operations is hardly sensible. For applications that need predictable failures, the RFC defines an error format. Its root element is patch-ops-error, containing one specific error element. Each carries a phrase attribute for human readers and, for most, the operation that failed.

The defined errors include unlocated-node (no single node found), invalid-attribute-value, invalid-character-set, invalid-diff-format, invalid-entity-declaration, invalid-namespace-prefix, invalid-namespace-uri, invalid-node-types, invalid-patch-directive, invalid-root-element-operation, invalid-xml-prolog-operation, invalid-whitespace-directive, unsupported-id-function and unsupported-xml-id. Extra errors from other namespaces may appear inside the root element.
sections.eli5: If the note says "change the third drawer" and there is no third drawer, the helper stops and tells you exactly what went wrong.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered a new XML namespace, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:patch-ops-error, and a new media type, application/patch-ops-error+xml, whose encoding rules follow application/xml as given in RFC 3023. It also registered two XML Schemas, urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:patch-ops for the operation types in Section 8 and urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:patch-ops-error for the errors in Section 9, using the procedures of RFC 3688.

The operation schema declares no target namespace, so its type definitions take on the namespace of the schema that includes it. Applications are expected to define their own add, replace and remove elements from these types, and may use only some of them.
sections.eli5: The authors put the new names in an official registry, so nobody else picks the same names for something different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says security depends heavily on the application that uses the framework, since each application has its own needs and threat model. One framework-specific risk is named: because it uses a limited subset of XPath 1.0, applications may be open to XPath injection attacks that reveal content a user should not see. These are most likely with shared resources where a user may only touch some parts.

The defence is that input MUST be sanitized, for example by validating diff documents against the restrictive schemas the RFC provides.
sections.eli5: If a stranger can write the address on the envelope, they might point it at a drawer they should not open, so you must check addresses before following them.

viz.caption: THE THREE PATCH OPERATIONS AND THEIR ATTRIBUTES

items.label: sel, type, pos
items.desc: Adds children, an attribute or a namespace declaration.

items.label: sel
items.desc: Replaces one node or node value with the new content.

items.label: sel, ws
items.desc: Removes a node, optionally with adjacent white space.

viz.caption: EXAMPLES OF THE THREE OPERATIONS, FROM SECTIONS 4.3.1, 4.4.2 AND 4.5.1

data.title: Patch operation elements
data.code:
<add sel="doc"><foo id="ert4773">This is a new child</foo></add>
<replace sel="doc/@a">new value</replace>
<remove sel="doc/foo[@a='1']" ws="after"/>
